newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans furious at drug censure by U.S. Congress.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans furious at drug censure by U.S. Congress.

text.p: Mexicans united on Thursday to condemn as unwarranted meddling a U.S. congressional decision to censure them for failing in the drug war.

The House of Representatives voted earlier in the day in Washington to deny Mexico an official seal of drug war approval unless President Bill Clinton reported within 90 days that progress had been made on a series of conditions.
The resolution must still clear the Senate and may face a presidential veto. It does not include economic sanctions but its message of public humiliation wounded Mexican pride.
The Mexican government rejected the decision as an "unacceptable" attempt to interfere in internal affairs which would hurt bilateral drug cooperation and only benefit traffickers.
"The resolution of the House of Representatives is sending a mistaken signal to Mexico and the world," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Thursday night.

"...The Government of Mexico reiterates that, in the event that this process should have consequences for the sovereignty, the dignity or the well-being of Mexicans, we will act with all the energy the situation demands."

Mexican officials expressed private concerns that if the drug decertification decision went through Congress, it could unleash so much anti-American sentiment that Clinton's planned visit here in April would be jeopardised.
"It's incredible how short-sighted Congress is," fumed one senior official. "This is creating a wave of anti-Americanism ...top business leaders here are mad."
"Right now preparations for the (Clinton) visit are going ahead but if this (certification row) goes on, then we could have an issue there," one official said.
Ordinary Mexicans, government officials, congressmen and business chiefs lost no time in venting their feelings.
"The gringos (Americans) think they have a divine right to do what they want. It's not right," said Juan Espinosa, 74, owner of a car repair shop in the upscale Lomas district.

"This 'yes' or 'no' pressure is damaging Mexico and as such is offensive for us," said industrialists' leader Carlos Gutierrez. "The process insults us -- it's very clear they don't want to recognise the (drug) effort we are making".
Caller Antonio Flores from the Mexico City suburb of Iztapalapa phoned a local radio station, Radio Red, with a message for President Ernesto Zedillo:
"If you call up Mexicans to defend national sovereignty, you can count on this humble Mexican. I don't have weapons or money but I have a great love for my country," he said.

Mexico has fought several wars with its giant northern neighbour and lost half its territory to the United States in the 19th century -- historical scars that lead Mexicans instinctively to mistrust Washington's intentions.
"The gringos are causing fear rather than respect because they are arrogant," said a 38-year-old nurse interviewed on the street. "They are wicked -- the gringos, the whole United States," she added.

Clinton himself criticised the House decision as the "wrong way" to go in the drug war, saying it would make life harder for President Zedillo to fight narcotics. The Mexican government statement thanked him for his support but "lamented" that congressmen did not share his good intentions.

Zedillo administration staff said the conditions imposed by Congress on them to win drug approval would be politically impossible to fulfil because they had been demanded in public. Accepting them would be seen here as caving in to Washington.
The demands include allowing U.S. anti-drug agents to carry weapons in Mexico and making progress toward allowing U.S. warships to pursue and arrest drug traffickers in Mexican waters.
